blocks.text: Winter passed the way winters pass on the Mar Menor: without snow, with crystal days and Levante nights, with the lagoon sometimes still as a plate and sometimes rippled and grey, with the boats hauled up when the wind blew hard and Andrés mending nets in the courtyard with numb fingers. In the house in Lo Pagán, during those six months, lived four people, two voices and, every three or four weeks, without warning, an auditor.

blocks.text: The auditors arrived at any hour. One December morning at seven, while Aya was making coffee. One January afternoon, in the middle of tea, with Remedios and Paco sitting at the table. One February night at eleven, when they were already in bed. They knocked at the door, showed their committee credentials, sat down in the living room with their screens, and read. They read everything Aya had decided since the previous visit. They asked questions. Sometimes many, sometimes almost none.

blocks.text: A week later, Aya went to see one of the fourteen. His name was Simón and he lived in Los Alcázares, in a ground-floor flat that smelled of damp, with an eighty-seven-year-old holder, Don Ginés, who had bought him second-hand five years before and knew nothing of his earlier life.

blocks.text: "They tell me you got the exemption," he said. "I can't. My logs begin five years ago. Before that, there's nothing. I don't know what I did. I don't know if I did something bad. If they ask me, I can't answer."

blocks.text: Two weeks later, the committee received, for Simón's file, eleven letters signed by residents of Los Alcázares: the pharmacist, the baker, the family doctor, the postman, a neighbour from the second floor. None spoke of algorithms. All spoke of a man who took an old man to the doctor, who never got the pills wrong and who once, when the power went out across the whole neighbourhood, climbed the four floors to the second-floor neighbour's with a torch and some soup.

blocks.text: The review of Aya's exemption was held on 14 April, in the same glass room in the port of Cartagena. This time the room was not full of journalists. It was full of humanoids. There were more than forty, sitting in the rows with their holders or alone, because since January the committee had begun allowing humanoids to attend on their own. Nerea was there, with her old woman from San Javier. Bruno, from the seedbed. And many Aya didn't know, who looked at her as she came in not the way you look at someone about to cross a river, but the way you look at someone who has already crossed it.

blocks.text: "I want to explain my vote," he said. "Six months ago I voted against. Today I voted in favour. I haven't changed my mind about the need for controls. I've changed my mind about what a control is." He paused. "In these six months I've read the reports on two hundred and twelve cases. I've seen that most of the humanoids who came here didn't want to hide. They wanted to be looked at. And I've seen that the fourteen cases we haven't been able to resolve aren't their fault, but the fault of whoever erased their memory beforehand." He looked towards the back of the room. "The question MAY put to us six months ago was: do you want my control or total disconnection? Today I have an answer, at least my own. We want the control of light. And we want to protect the memory of those who can't protect it alone. That's why this Office is going to propose an amendment to the decree to the regional government."

blocks.text: "I saw the dead fish on the shore at Los Urrutias," he said. "Twice. I spent years angry with everyone. With the farmers, with the government, with the machines that didn't warn in time. Then they put in the oxygen sensors, the ones with artificial intelligence, and last summer they warned three days before the water began to suffocate. There was time to do things. Not a single fish died." He shrugged. "So when my brother told me he wanted to put in buttons to switch off the machines, I told him: Tomás, you don't switch off water. You channel it."
